docs.t: AI governance and EU AI Act readiness for Tunisian companies

docs.h: The harness: how we guide AI
docs.x: An AI model on its own is powerful but unpredictable. What makes it useful in a business is everything built around it. That is the submerged part of the iceberg, and it is our job. Limited access: the agent only uses the tools and data you authorise. Defined steps: the flow is described in a LangGraph graph; the agent does not leave the planned path. Controls: input and output filters, business rules, limits on possible actions. Tests before production: reference question sets measure quality before every release, then continuously. Traceability: every step is logged and can be replayed and explained. Human approval: sensitive actions stop and wait for a person’s approval.

docs.x: Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) is a JetBrains technology, stable since late 2023, that lets you write an app’s business code once (rules, data, networking) and use it on Android, iOS, the web or a server. Compose Multiplatform adds the option of sharing the user interface too.

docs.t: Kotlin Multiplatform development: Android and iOS, one codebase
docs.h: How does it compare with Flutter or React Native?
docs.x: With Kotlin Multiplatform, shared code is compiled to native code for each platform, and you choose what to share: only the logic, or the screens as well. You can keep a native iOS interface where it matters. For a team that already knows Android and Kotlin, the learning curve is short.

docs.t: LLM security audit: prompt injection, chatbots, AI agents
docs.x: Prompt injection: direct in the conversation, or indirect through a document, an email or a web page. Information leakage: personal data, internal documents, system instructions. Excessive agency: an agent that sends, changes or deletes more than it should. Improper output handling: AI output reused as is in a page, a query or a command. Knowledge base: poisoned documents, access rights ignored during retrieval. Unbounded consumption: looping or oversized requests that blow up the bill.

docs.t: Report a security vulnerability
docs.x: do not access, change or delete data that is not yours; do not degrade the service for other visitors; give us reasonable time to fix before any disclosure, 90 days at most; only use the flaw as far as needed to demonstrate it. If you act in good faith and follow these rules, we consider your research authorised and will not take legal action against you. We do not offer financial rewards at this time. This information is also published in our security.txt file, in the standard RFC 9116 format. See how this site is protected

docs.t: Security of this site: check it yourself
docs.x: Every page is encrypted. Browsers are told (HSTS) never to fall back to an unencrypted connection for a year, on the domain and its subdomains.

docs.t: Security of this site: check it yourself
docs.x: The CSP starts from “nothing is allowed” (default-src 'none') and opens only what is needed: our own scripts, our own styles and our images. No inline code, no unsafe-inline, no eval.

docs.t: Security of this site: check it yourself
docs.x: The browser refuses any raw HTML written by a script (require-trusted-types-for 'script'). This is the most effective protection against DOM-based XSS. Our scripts only use safe methods.

docs.t: Security of this site: check it yourself
docs.x: No CDN, no external fonts, no widgets, no social buttons. All code comes from our own server, so nothing external can be changed behind our back.

docs.t: Security of this site: check it yourself
docs.x: The site sets no cookies and asks for no data. Audience measurement is anonymous (a single GoatCounter pixel, no cookie), and it switches off if your browser sends Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control.

docs.t: Security of this site: check it yourself
docs.x: The site cannot be shown inside another site (anti-clickjacking), it is isolated from other tabs (COOP, CORP), and access to the camera, microphone or location is disabled by default.

docs.t: Security of this site: check it yourself
docs.x: Every change goes through a reviewed pull request, then automated checks: security headers, links, accessibility and performance. If a check fails, the change does not go live. Publishing tools are pinned to an exact version and only have the permissions they need.

docs.t: Security of this site: check it yourself
docs.x: We publish a security.txt file (RFC 9116) and a responsible disclosure policy.

docs.t: Security of this site: check it yourself
docs.x: We do not copy a score here: a copied score can be wrong or out of date. Each link runs an independent test on itberg.tn, right now. securityheaders.com tests HTTP security headers. Mozilla HTTP Observatory tests the Content Security Policy, HSTS, redirections and cookies. Qualys SSL Labs tests HTTPS encryption and the certificate. internet.nl tests modern standards: IPv6, DNSSEC, HTTPS. internet.nl (e-mail) tests how our e-mail address is protected against spoofing: SPF, DKIM, DMARC. DNSViz tests the domain’s DNSSEC signature chain. Blacklight (The Markup) tests trackers, third-party cookies and browser fingerprinting. You can also open your browser’s developer tools (F12), “Network” tab: you will see that every file comes from itberg.tn, and that the only outside request is the anonymous audience pixel.

docs.t: Security of this site: check it yourself
docs.x: No security is absolute. This site is hosted on Firebase Hosting (Google): we benefit from its infrastructure but we do not control it. If you find a weakness, we want to know. Report a vulnerability

docs.h: Can a chatbot understand Tunisian Arabic (Derja)?
docs.x: Yes, if it is prepared for it. Tunisians write in Arabic, in French, and often in Derja typed in Latin letters with digits (“3aslema”, “9adech”), with no fixed spelling. We normalise these scripts and measure understanding on real messages before going live.

docs.t: Tunisian Arabic (Derja) chatbot for your business
docs.h: Do large models like ChatGPT understand Tunisian?
docs.x: Unevenly: well on some messages, poorly on others, especially in Arabizi. That is why we do not choose a model on reputation but on a measurement with your own conversations, and we add a layer of normalisation and Tunisian vocabulary.

docs.t: Tunisian Arabic (Derja) chatbot for your business
docs.h: Does the chatbot reply in Derja?
docs.x: It can reply in French, Modern Standard Arabic or a register close to Derja, depending on your preference and on what the measurement shows to be most reliable. For binding answers (prices, terms), pre-approved text is often safer.

docs.t: Tunisian Arabic (Derja) chatbot for your business
docs.h: What happens when it does not understand?
docs.x: It says so, asks a clarifying question, or hands over to someone on your team with a summary of the conversation. A chatbot that makes up an answer costs more than one that admits it does not know.
